brief.headline: Funding is cheap, collateral is not: the bill arrives through defaults, not spreads.
brief.summary: CLO liabilities are pricing at the year's tights — refi/reset AAA at [[F02]] — while the collateral underneath deteriorates: Fitch's European loan default rate has climbed to [[F30]] and the Market Concern list stands at [[F35]], the highest since early 2013. The market is paying up for safety at the top of the stack and under-charging for loss at the bottom. Two named credits carry the event risk: **Altice International** (litigation-led) and **Thames Water** (runway-led). Our stance: harvest manager selection in seasoned mezzanine, veto the junior event names, and buy the data we lack.

topics.title: CLO liabilities vs arbitrage — the market pays managers to refinance, not to buy
topics.thesis: Liability spreads sit at the year's tights while asset spreads compress: the arbitrage favours resets of old deals over new equity.
topics.stance: Prefer seasoned mezzanine over primary equity
topics.stack_note: Tranche shares are a teaching example; the one market number attached is the AAA price — new issue near [[F01]] in September. Equity owns the residual, so asset-spread compression lands on the bottom tranche first.
topics.signal: September broke a three-month run of repricing dominance: new issue printed [[F04]] against [[F05]] of refi/reset, taking year-to-date issuance to [[F03]]. AAA new issue averaged [[F01]] while refi/reset AAA cleared at [[F02]] — the year's tightest — a gap of only [[F08]]. BofA still expects around [[F06]] of refi/reset for the full year.
topics.mechanism: Equity is the residual of the asset spread minus the weighted cost of liabilities, fees and expected losses. With loan spreads near [[F07]] and repricing waves still cutting collateral coupons, much of each basis point saved on the AAA is clawed back on the asset side. That is why managers prefer resetting existing liabilities, and why new equity is increasingly captive (manager-sponsored equity funds) rather than third-party. BB pricing is dispersing by manager: tiering, not beta, is the trade.
topics.latex_note: s = spread, w = tranche weight, f = management fees, ℓ = expected credit loss. A practitioner's excess-spread approximation, not a deal model: it ignores reinvestment, OC diversion and timing. When asset spreads fall faster than the weighted liability cost, equity cash-on-cash compresses even at record-tight AAA levels. No liability weights or fee loads were captured this cycle, so it is not evaluated numerically.
factors: Institutional demand for AAA (CLO ETFs, insurers under Solvency II) keeps the senior bid firm.
Loan repricing waves cut collateral coupons faster than liabilities can be reset.
Captive equity funds lower the bar for printing marginal new deals.
Manager tiering widens BB dispersion — selection matters more than the index.
Rising defaults (T4) erode par and junior OC cushions; trustee data is needed to measure it (gap G1).

scenarios.label: Senior bid breaks

topics.posture: Do not underwrite primary equity at today's arbitrage. Prefer seasoned BBB/BB mezzanine from top-tier managers bought in secondary, where dispersion pays for selection. Treat the AAA level as a funding-cost signal, not a return source.
topics.verify: October CLO print (early November): the new-issue versus refi mix, the AAA average and any widening in BB dispersion. Confirm the asset-spread figure from a primary source — today it is low-confidence at [[F07]].

topics.title: Altice International — same sponsor, same playbook, new battlefield
topics.thesis: Altice France is finished; the fight has moved to Altice International, where asset designations and a default notice have put recovery into court.
topics.signal: Altice France closed its restructuring: debt cut by roughly [[F10]], leverage to about [[F11]], creditors taking about [[F12]] of the equity. The contest has moved to Altice International. In November 2025 Altice Portugal and Altice Caribbean were designated unrestricted and new money of [[F16]] was raised against them. The 2028 secured group served a default notice on [[F13]]; an action is now before the New York Supreme Court. Roughly [[F15]] of secured debt is in play, about [[F14]] matures in 2027, and the bonds trade in the [[F17]].
topics.mechanism: The playbook is value migration: move crown-jewel assets outside the restricted group by unrestricted-subsidiary designation, raise priming new money against them, then negotiate from strength with the creditors left behind. Recovery for the legacy secured group becomes a function of the collateral left in the box, the court's reading of the indenture, and how hard the maturity wall presses the sponsor.
topics.latex_note: A decision-analysis framing, not a market pricing formula: P_win is the probability the court unwinds or penalises the designations; c_lit is litigation and time cost. None of the inputs is observable today and no price is captured (gap G4), so it structures the question rather than answering it.
factors: Indenture capacity for unrestricted-subsidiary designations and asset-transfer baskets.
The New York court timetable and any interim relief.
The 2027 maturity wall forcing the sponsor to the table.
Cohesion of the secured creditors' cooperation agreement.
CLO read-across: downgrades into CCC push holdings into the excess-CCC haircut and erode OC tests.

topics.title: Thames Water — junior recovery near zero, even by consent
topics.thesis: The Class B outcome is now consensual but brutal; the live risk has moved to liquidity runway and political tolerance.
topics.stance: Hard veto on junior WBS paper
topics.signal: The Class B Transaction Support Agreement is backed by holders of [[F22]] of the roughly [[F23]] outstanding: a full write-off in exchange for about [[F24]] recovered via equity, plus rights to join a [[F25]] equity raise. Liquidity is the binding constraint: [[F20]] of the emergency facility is drawn, cash runs out around late 2026 to early 2027, and the company is asking for a further [[F21]] to last into autumn 2027 — a request that worries super-senior holders about dilution. The London & Valley Water consortium (Elliott, Silver Point) proposes Lord Hutton as chair-designate.
topics.mechanism: Whole-business securitisation protects senior creditors through ring-fencing and step-in rights, but the regulator's tolerance sets the ceiling. A recapitalisation needs Ofwat concessions on penalties, the investment programme and returns; without them the Special Administration Regime becomes the political default. SAR protects service continuity, not creditor value, and freezes timelines.
topics.latex: R_{\text{junior}} = \frac{\max\left(0,\; V_{\text{EV}} - D_{\text{super-senior}} - D_{\text{Class A}}\right)}{D_{\text{Class B}}}
topics.latex_note: Junior recovery is the residual after super-senior and Class A claims under strict absolute priority. Real outcomes are negotiated: the Class B TSA grants an equity recovery even though the residual may be zero, which is exactly the deviation this identity exposes. No enterprise value was captured this cycle.
factors: Ofwat concessions on penalties and the investment programme.
Size and seniority of incremental super-senior funding.
Political appetite for SAR versus a creditor-led recapitalisation.
Class A holders' acceptance of extension and haircut terms.
Read-across to other UK water whole-business securitisations.

topics.title: The default cycle is turning — quietly, through the back door
topics.thesis: Defaults are rising faster than forecasters expected, and the channel is repeat defaults and LMEs rather than headline bankruptcies.
topics.stance: Raise default assumptions; respect the OC maths
topics.signal: Fitch's European leveraged loan trailing default rate reached [[F30]] in September, up from [[F31]] in August and [[F32]] at mid-year. In July Fitch raised its full-year forecast to [[F33]] from [[F34]]. The Market Concern list — loans Fitch sees at risk of default — stands at [[F35]], the highest since early 2013. Repeat defaults and liability-management exercises are a material driver across an index of [[F40]].
topics.mechanism: LMEs count as defaults when they impose losses, but they often leave the borrower alive and inside CLO portfolios at lower ratings. The damage arrives through CCC buckets and par erosion rather than through a wave of liquidations. When CCC holdings exceed the permitted bucket, the excess is carried at market value in OC tests; failing a junior OC test diverts cash from equity and mezzanine to deleveraging.
topics.latex_note: The market-standard shape of a CLO overcollateralisation test, simplified: each indenture defines its own haircuts, carrying values and trigger levels. Performing par plus defaulted assets at market value, less the haircut on CCC holdings above the bucket, over the par of tranche j and everything senior to it. Junior OC is where a rising default rate bites first — trustee data is the missing input (gap G1).
factors: Repeat defaults among previously restructured borrowers.
LME prevalence in sponsor-backed capital structures.
Software and AI-exposed sectors facing revenue-model pressure.
Refinancing wall for weaker credits over the next two years.
Speed of rating migration into CCC.

scenarios.label: Steady climb
scenarios.text: The trailing rate moves into the forecast range by year-end; losses are absorbed by OC cushions.

scenarios.label: Plateau
scenarios.text: Repricing relief and amend-and-extend hold the rate near current levels.

scenarios.label: Acceleration
scenarios.text: Market Concern names default in a cluster and junior OC tests trip across vintages.
scenarios.kill_switch: Two consecutive monthly prints each rising by more than half a percentage point.

topics.posture: Underwrite European loan portfolios at the top of Fitch's forecast range, not at the trailing rate. Favour CLOs with clean collateral and junior OC headroom — which requires trustee data before any commitment (decision D2).
topics.verify: Fitch's monthly default update (mid-November); rating migration into CCC; LME announcements among sponsor-backed borrowers.

topics.title: Private credit — 'bad PIK' is the shadow default rate
topics.thesis: PIK switched on after origination signals cash-flow stress that headline default rates miss — and there is still no reliable public series to measure it.
topics.stance: Demand PIK disclosure before any allocation
topics.signal: Advisers and regulators distinguish good PIK, structured at origination, from bad PIK, switched on later to preserve liquidity. Commentary concentrates stress in 2021–22 vintages and in software and SaaS borrowers exposed to AI disruption. No quantified public series of bad-PIK incidence was found this cycle (gap G3).
topics.mechanism: A coupon converted to PIK preserves the borrower's cash but grows the claim: loan-to-value drifts up while the loan stays 'performing'. Marks lag, so NAV-based reporting understates stress until a realisation event — refinancing, sale or default — forces price discovery.
topics.latex_note: Compounding arithmetic, exact by construction: under PIK the claim grows while enterprise value may stagnate, so LTV rises without a single missed payment. No PIK rates or valuations were captured (gap G3).
factors: Share of portfolio income received in kind versus in cash.
Amendment frequency and covenant resets.
Vintage concentration at 2021–22 entry valuations.
Sector exposure to AI-driven disruption (software and SaaS).
Valuation governance: who marks, how often, on what evidence.

scenarios.label: Slow burn
scenarios.text: Bad PIK rises gradually and is absorbed through amendments; markdowns stay selective.

scenarios.label: Realisation wave
scenarios.text: Refinancings and sales force markdowns on the weakest vintages.

scenarios.label: Liquidity contagion
scenarios.text: Redemption pressure in semi-liquid vehicles forces asset sales.
scenarios.kill_switch: Gating or redemption limits at a major semi-liquid private credit vehicle.

topics.posture: No allocation without manager disclosure of the PIK split (origination versus amendment) and vintage concentration. Treat the absence of a series as a risk in itself.
topics.verify: Source a quantified PIK series from BDC filings and rating-agency private credit default studies (gap G3); watch redemption data at semi-liquid vehicles.

topics.title: Bank of England — layered leverage and AI capex debt share the same balance sheets
topics.thesis: The FPC keeps private credit and leveraged lending on its vulnerability list, and now links AI capex financing to the same channels.
topics.signal: The Financial Policy Committee continues to flag private credit and leveraged lending as vulnerabilities: opacity, layered leverage, and a maturity wall managed through amend-and-extend. It highlights that AI-related capex is increasingly financed through private credit, leveraged finance and structured finance. Its system-wide exploratory scenario work is mapping how non-bank stress transmits.
topics.mechanism: Leverage multiplies through layers: a fund borrows against its NAV, the portfolio company is itself levered, and the lender may be financed by bank back-leverage. Each layer looks modest; the product does not. Shocks transmit through margin calls and redemptions rather than direct defaults.
topics.latex_note: A stylised illustration of how exposure compounds across layers (fund NAV facility × portfolio-company leverage × lender back-leverage). It is not a Bank of England metric and is not calibrated: no layer multiples were captured this cycle.
factors: FPC and PRA supervisory focus on bank lending to non-banks.
Concentration of AI capex financing in a small set of sponsors and supply chains.
NAV-facility usage by private equity funds.
Margin and liquidity terms on back-leverage.
Coordination with the ECB and FSB on non-bank leverage.

scenarios.label: Supervisory pressure
scenarios.text: More disclosure requests; no binding limits.

scenarios.label: Targeted measures
scenarios.text: Capital or reporting requirements on bank lending to non-banks.

scenarios.label: Market event
scenarios.text: Stress at a large AI-capex borrower or fund forces de-leveraging across layers.
scenarios.kill_switch: A disorderly fund wind-down or a margin-call cascade reported by the Bank of England.

topics.posture: No direct position. Use as the systemic overlay: hold a convex hedge on European high yield (opportunity O2), sized to the portfolio's exposure to layered structures.
topics.verify: The next FPC record and the ECB Financial Stability Review (expected late November); published SWES findings.

heuristics.text: A claim that cannot be traced to a capture note is not a figure; it is a gap.
Liability tights are a funding signal, not a return; read the arbitrage from the asset side.
In sponsor situations, follow the assets out of the restricted group before reading the price.
Regulated-utility recoveries are set by the regulator's tolerance, not by the waterfall alone.
LMEs default borrowers into CCC buckets, not into liquidation — watch OC, not headlines.
An estimate without a resolve-by date is an opinion: date it or drop it.
